explanations.answer: He visited uncircumcised men and ate with them
explanations.explanation: That's the complaint. The circumcised believers tell Peter, one of Jesus' apostles, “You visited uncircumcised men and ate with them.” Notice they don't say a word about the trip itself. It's about who he sat down with at the table. I think Peter felt that one, because nobody likes being called out over who they ate with.

explanations.answer: He baptized people without asking the apostles
explanations.explanation: Nope, baptizing isn't what they bring up. The text says the circumcised believers took issue with Peter and said, “You visited uncircumcised men and ate with them.” Their complaint is about where he went and who he ate with. Nobody in this scene mentions a baptism rule.

explanations.answer: He stayed away from Jerusalem far too long
explanations.explanation: That would sound like a text from a worried friend, wouldn't it? But the believers say nothing about how long Peter was gone. What they say is, “You visited uncircumcised men and ate with them.” The trouble was the company he kept, not the calendar.

Not quite, friend. Peter doesn't refuse and he doesn't walk out. The text says Peter “…began and explained to them the whole sequence of events…” (Acts 11:4). He stays put and tells it from the start.

Right, he stays. Acts 11:4 says Peter “…began and explained to them the whole sequence of events…” He doesn't dodge the question or head for the door. He lays the whole thing out, one piece at a time. When people take issue with you, a calm explanation beats a dramatic exit.

That's the one. Peter says he was praying in Joppa and, in a trance, saw “…something like a large sheet being let down from heaven by its four corners…” Notice he says “something like.” He's describing what he saw as honestly as he can. And it came right down to him (Acts 11:5).

A basket would at least have handles, friend. But Peter says what he saw was “…something like a large sheet…” It was let down from heaven by its four corners, and it came right down to him. The corners are the clue that points to a sheet.

Good guess, friend. But that's not what Peter describes. He says he saw “…something like a large sheet being let down from heaven by its four corners…” No net in his telling. Just something like a large sheet coming down to where he was.

explanations.answer: Get up and kill and eat
explanations.explanation: That's what Peter hears. He tells the believers, “Then I heard a voice saying to me, ‘Get up, Peter, kill and eat.’” The voice calls him by name and gives a plain command. And there's the sheet full of animals right in front of him. I think Peter's jaw hit the floor.

explanations.answer: Lead them up to the temple
explanations.explanation: A temple trip? Not in this vision, friend. Peter says the voice told him, “Get up, Peter, kill and eat.” The voice doesn't send him anywhere. It speaks about the animals on the sheet, right in front of him, and I think Peter would have loved a temple errand about then.
I think that would've made things a lot easier for Peter. But the voice says something else. Peter reports it as “Get up, Peter, kill and eat.” That command is the one he pushes back on next.

explanations.answer: Nothing impure has ever entered his mouth
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's his reason. Peter answers, “No, Lord,” and then says, “for nothing impure or unclean has ever entered my mouth.” He's honest about it, even while talking to the Lord. Then the voice speaks again, and what it says changes the whole conversation (Acts 11:9).

explanations.answer: He has been fasting since early that morning
explanations.explanation: The text never says Peter was fasting. His reason is different: “for nothing impure or unclean has ever entered my mouth.” It's about what he has and hasn't eaten in his whole life, not about one morning. Stick with what he actually says.

explanations.answer: He has never killed an animal himself
explanations.explanation: Peter doesn't say anything about who has or hasn't killed an animal. He tells the Lord, “No, Lord, for nothing impure or unclean has ever entered my mouth.” I think most of us would have argued about the killing part first. But Peter's concern is what goes into his mouth, and that's the reason in the text.

True. Peter says, “But the voice spoke from heaven a second time, ‘Do not call anything impure that God has made clean.’” Notice the voice doesn't let his answer be the last word. It speaks again, plain and clear. I've had to hear things twice myself, and I never had a voice from heaven doing it.

It's actually true. Peter tells the believers that the voice spoke from heaven a second time. The words were, “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean.” So Peter's “No, Lord” gets a second answer. Hold onto that line, because the rest of the story leans on it.

That's it. Peter says, “The Spirit told me to accompany them without hesitation.” Three men show up at the door, and the Spirit says go, no dragging his feet. After the vision he'd just had, I bet that one clicked into place. And six brothers went along with him too.
The Spirit says the opposite. Peter reports that the Spirit told him to accompany the three men without hesitation. So Peter doesn't send anybody home. He goes with them.
That's not what the Spirit says. Peter reports that the Spirit told him to accompany the men “without hesitation.” Holding them back isn't anywhere in the Spirit's word. The word was to go with them.

True. Peter tells them the man “told us how he had seen an angel standing in his house and saying, ‘Send to Joppa for Simon who is called Peter.’” The man was Cornelius (Acts 10:1), and the angel gave him Peter's name. That's how a houseful of Gentiles ends up with an apostle at the door.

It's true, friend. The man who told Peter and the others this was Cornelius (Acts 10:1), and he said he saw an angel standing in his house. The angel said, “Send to Joppa for Simon who is called Peter.” So Peter was asked for by name. Not a bad way to get an invitation.

The same. Peter says the Holy Spirit fell upon them “…just as He had fallen upon us at the beginning.” He lines the two moments up with “just as.” A few verses later he calls it “…the same gift…” (Acts 11:17). There's no ranking in this story.

Peter says nothing like that. He says the Holy Spirit fell on them “…just as He had fallen upon us at the beginning.” Just as. He doesn't hint that they got less than the believers did. In verse 17 he says God gave them “…the same gift…”

Peter doesn't say that either. He says the Holy Spirit fell upon them “…just as He had fallen upon us at the beginning.” It's an even match, no bigger and no smaller. He calls it “…the same gift…” in Acts 11:17.

explanations.answer: Who was he to hinder God's work
explanations.explanation: That's his question. Peter says, “So if God gave them the same gift He gave us who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I to hinder the work of God?” He doesn't ask them to vote on it. He asks who he is to stand in the way. That's a humble thing to say.

Peter never asks that, friend. He asks, “…who was I to hinder the work of God?” He's pointing to what God has already done by giving them the same gift. Circumcision doesn't come up in his answer, and I think that's the point: when God has already acted, who is Peter to add a step?

Peter doesn't ask for a ruling from anyone. His question is, “…who was I to hinder the work of God?” He's an apostle himself, and he sees that God has already acted. So he turns the question back on the room.

Not this time. Acts 11:18 says, “When they heard this, they had no further objections…” They had taken issue with Peter, and now there's nothing left to object to. Once they heard it, the objections stopped.

False is right. The text says, “When they heard this, they had no further objections…” Peter told them the whole sequence of events, and it settled things. The same people who took issue with him are the ones who stop objecting.

That's what they do. The text says they “glorified God, saying, ‘So then, God has granted even the Gentiles repentance unto life.’” They went from objecting to praising. And the praise is about what God did, not about who won the argument.

Nope, nobody sends for Cornelius in this verse. The text says that when they heard Peter, they had no further objections and “glorified God.” Their response is praise, and I think that's quite a turn from where they started in verse 2. Nobody sends anyone anywhere here.
No second meeting is mentioned. Acts 11:18 says they had no further objections, and “…they glorified God…” They don't add a committee. They praise God right there.
